questions.q: What is opportunity cost, as the summary describes it?
a: What else you could have bought with the same money
The interest you pay on a credit card
The discount you lose by not comparing prices
The fee a broker charges for a purchase
questions.why: Lesson 1 says we rarely ask what else that money could buy, which is the cost economists call opportunity cost.

questions.q: How do companies make spending feel less painful, according to the summary?
a: They separate payment from consumption and add rewards
They lower prices only for loyal customers
They hide the full price until checkout
They offer free returns on every purchase
questions.why: Lesson 1 explains that retailers stretch the gap between paying and consuming and hand out points or miles.

A promise to repay a loan by a fixed date
An agreement between two people to share costs
A savings account with a high interest rate
questions.why: Lesson 2 compares it to Ulysses tying himself to the mast, a system that removes the option of giving in.

questions.q: Which budgeting approach do the authors recommend?
a: A simple limit on discretionary spending
A detailed spreadsheet for every category
Tracking each purchase in a mobile app
Reviewing your spending once a year
questions.why: Lesson 3 says complicated budgets get abandoned, so set a prudent allowance for non-essentials and stick to it.

questions.q: What exercise does the summary suggest for connecting with your future self?
a: Picture your retired self thanking you
Write a budget for your retirement years
Calculate your likely pension income
Ask older relatives about their regrets
questions.why: Lesson 2 says imagining your future self enjoying retirement makes long-term saving feel more real.
